description:
We are an engineering, software, and design team building M.A.R.V.I.S. (Mars Augmented Reality Visual Instrumentation System) for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 (Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map). 

Combining geospatial data science, human physiology modeling, and real-time Unity simulation, we bridge mission-control planning with autonomous astronaut survival on Mars.
summary:
February 6th 1971, 10:41 GMT, Shephard and Mitchell had reached the highest point of their trek in Apollo 14's second moonwalk when mission control realized that neither of them had enough oxygen to continue the mission. Both astronauts had to return preemptively because oxygen reserve calculations hadn't considered how trek difficulty would impact their metabolic rates. Far from home small mistakes can mean the end of the mission, or worse. This is where M.A.R.V.I.S. (Mars Augmented Reality Visual Instrumentation System) comes in; a mission control and heads up display (HUD) that enables astronauts to conduct EVAs safely and efficiently in Aeolis Mons. This is done by providing astronauts with comprehensive mission planning tools which consider environmental and physiological factors as well as live mapping, route planning, and health data through the HUD. 

To aid in research efforts, the astronaut will have layered mapping data for material composition and set key points of interest available in the map. While research is the goal, Mars can be a rough and unforgiving environment, which means that astronauts will need route planning that considers speed, oxygen, temperature, and weather; efficiency is speed with a good safety margin.

Running this workflow in a Unity simulation allows us to also port this system for training purposes on Earth in such a way that astronauts can learn to use the mission planning and heads up displays before taking on the first marswalk.
details:
M.A.R.V.I.S. is a mission control suite and astronaut heads-up display (HUD) that makes Marswalks safer and more productive in Aeolis Mons, Gale Crater. It runs as a Unity simulation with two connected halves built on a single, shared human physiology model:

M.A.R.V.I.S. Consists of two elements:

1. The Mission Control Planner: A planning tool that builds EVA routes from real NASA terrain, mineral, weather and radiation data to find the safest and most scientifically rewarding paths.

2. The Astronaut HUD & Simulation: A first-person simulation where an astronaut can preform science based experiments while following a planned route with a live HUD.

Part 1: Plan the EVA (Mission Control)

1. Terrain & Hazard Mapping Using real elevation, weather, radiation, mineral composition and satellite imagery of Gale Crater, M.A.R.V.I.S. generates a layered 3D map that can be toggled to fit the mission profile. It uses topological data to flag dangerous terrain. Slopes over 20° are blocked entirely, slopes between 17° and 20° are marked as beyond tested spacesuit limits, and any area missing high-resolution data is marked "unknown" and never routed through.

2. Health data modelled, every single step Walking in a pressurised spacesuit on Mars is exhausting, especially uphill or across rocky ridges. At the core of Mission Control is a metabolic model built on NASA spacesuit research: for every step it works out how fast a suited astronaut can safely walk on that slope, how much oxygen their muscles burn climbing it, and how much braking costs on the way down, all in Martian gravity. Speed is capped by limiters such as the terrain or the astronaut's own aerobic ceiling. The model is run in different suit masses and different physiology scenarios (optimistic, nominal and conservative), so every number in the planner comes with its uncertainty band.

  • Terrain model: Instead of drawing a simple flat circle around the Pad, M.A.R.V.I.S. calculates the true reachable area, based on the topological map. A reverse shortest-path search runs outward from each candidate landing pad across more than 4 million 3 m terrain cells, in 16 directions, so routes can follow ridges and switchbacks instead of a coarse grid. For every single cell it stores the fastest way home, the walking time and the oxygen it costs, and checks reachability against multiple independent margins like oxygen reserve, daylight, total EVA time and radiation dose. The mission planners can create detailed route, including multiple waypoints, this is compiled into a mission profile, determining how far an astronaut can walk and still safely return with a given safety margin. Because of the steep terrain, a crew can reach and safely return from only 23% of the area a flat 30-minute circle would suggest (15–29% across scenarios).
  • Real-Time Route Planning: Because the heavy lifting is already done, planning becomes interactive. Mission planners pick a precomputed landing pad, then drag and drop science stations and free waypoints onto the 3D map. A heuristic search, guided by the precomputed return-home maps, routes every leg across the terrain in a fraction of a second, and the full mission profile updates live: walking time, oxygen used, oxygen left, and the safety margin over the whole EVA. If a plan breaks a limit, the planner shows exactly which leg fails and which margin it violates, so unsafe missions are caught before anyone steps outside. The official mission plans are then verified by the full planning engine against the same model.
  • Partner Haul Range Because astronauts walk in pairs, M.A.R.V.I.S. also shows a rescue range: how far a crew could bring back an incapacitated partner on a cart. Dragging a suited astronaut by hand turns out to be impossible on Mars, because it needs more force than boot grip can provide.

3. Scientific Research M.A.R.V.I.S. scores potential science sites based on mineral deposits (clays and sulphates) and geological formations, paired with photos from past Curiosity Rover images, to optimize scientific research.

  • POI's (Points Of Interest): Mission planners can drag and drop science stations on the 3D map, and M.A.R.V.I.S. recalculates the entire route, oxygen usage, and latest safe turn-back time in real time.
  • Field Science & Rover Rendezvous: Astronauts can follow the real path driven by NASA’s Curiosity rover, viewing past photos, and a heatmap of previously explored territory.

Part 2: Simulate The EVA.

1. First-Person Marswalk: Astronauts can step into the planned mission in a first-person Unity simulation covering a 6.1 × 6.1 km patch of Gale Crater, complete with 1:1 rock formations including accurate mineral compositions scanned by Curiosity, planet curvature, and Mars gravity. Crews can replay planned routes at up to 300× speed or walk freely using the exact same helmet HUD they would wear on Mars.

2. Live Vitals, Maps & Sky Navigation:

  • Real-Time Oxygen & Biometrics: As the astronaut walks, the HUD tracks live oxygen burn, heart rate, and ECG traces. Walking the planned route matches the mission planner’s oxygen predictions within 1%.
  • Helmet Maps: A compass dial points the way home, while a full visor map lets the crew toggle between slope, mineral, weather, and satellite layers.
  • Star Tracking: Because Mars has no global magnetic field for a standard compass, the HUD simulates over 5,000 real stars, constellations, planets, and Mars's moons (Phobos and Deimos) dimmed accurately by atmospheric dust to help crews navigate.

3. Field Science & Rover Rendezvous:

Astronauts can follow the real path driven by NASA’s Curiosity rover, and meet the rover on the surface. Using a handheld rock scanner, crews can aim at boulders to inspect their chemical makeup and mineral spectra based on real Curiosity samples. (each rock is a 1:1 replica of its counterpart on mars).

Part 3: When Things Go Wrong.

1. Dust Storms & Solar Radiation M.A.R.V.I.S. simulates five weather states: from clear skies to blinding dust storms, using real Martian wind audio and dust-devil observations. It also replays a real solar storm event, if radiation spikes above safe levels, an automated tripwire alerts the crew 22 minutes before the storm peaks.

2. Stress & Low-Clutter Alarms Battling heavy winds, cold temperatures, and steep slopes spikes the astronaut's heart rate and accelerates oxygen burn. To prevent information overload during an emergency, the HUD displays only one alarm at a time in order of urgency.

Impact, Validation & Next Steps

  • Built for Safety & Reuse: M.A.R.V.I.S. prioritizes survival alongside speed, refuses to start unsafe missions, and can be adapted to any planetary site with elevation and mineral data, including the Moon.
  • System Reliability: Verified by 342 unit tests, 47 automated self-checks, and 1,291 known-answer tests. Simulated elements (weather, vitals, and analogue rock data) are clearly labelled on-screen so crews never confuse simulated telemetry with live measurements.
  • Next Steps: Validate the physiology model against physical spacesuit field trials, expand to new Martian landing sites, and test the HUD with human crews in Earth-analogue environments.

Technical Appendix: NASA Data, Equations & Specifications

  • Terrain & Mapping: USGS MSL Gale merged elevation model (1 m resolution gridded to 3 m via Horn plane fit) combining HiRISE, CTX, and MOLA (NASA) with HRSC imagery (ESA). Ground-truthed against 537 Curiosity rover drive positions (0.037 m residual error, zero shift).
  • Minerals & Geology: CRISM orbital spectrometer indices (SINDEX2 for sulfates, D2300 for clays), 15 m median-filtered ridge density for boxwork formations, and 32 real Curiosity rock analyses from APXS, CheMin, and ChemCam via the Planetary Data System (PDS).
  • Weather & Radiation: Curiosity RAD (replaying the 20 May 2024 solar storm, peaking at 0.35 mGy/h), REMS surface temperatures, Mastcam dust opacity, and Spirit / Perseverance dust devil and microphone wind data.
  • Astronomy & Time: NASA HEASARC Bright Star Catalogue (5,080 stars to magnitude 6 across 88 constellations), JPL ephemerides, NAIF planetary orientation model, and the Mars24 solar time algorithm (accurate within 5 seconds).

Physiology, Engineering & Software Specs

  • Oxygen & Effort Model (NASA ICES-2026-127): V02 anchored at 19 mL/kg/min for suited walking at 0.98 m/s in Mars gravity (3.72 m/s²), assuming 22.5% uphill muscle efficiency, downhill braking curves, and a speed limiter capped at the lower of slope limits (1.0, 0.6, or 0.3 m/s) or 50% of V02 Max (36 mL/kg/min). Calculated across optimistic, nominal, and conservative variants for 80, 104, and 120 kg suits.
  • Reachability & Margins: Reverse Dijkstra search (16 directions) yields a reachable 30-minute zone of 15–29% (23% nominal) of the flat-ground circle. Oxygen margin requires a 40.5 L reserve (30 min at max effort of 1.35 L/min), station work burns 0.84 L/min (1,000 BTU/h). Simulated HUD walk matches planner O2 within ~1% (126.17 L vs. 124.87 L).
  • Partner Haul & Radiation Limits: Haul force shows dragging a 179 kg suited astronaut requires 398 N vs. 351 N of available boot traction. Radiation tripwire triggers at >3× baseline for two consecutive samples (22 min before peak), dose leash allows ~86 min at peak (0.5 mGy limit).
  • Simulation & Software Stack: 6.1 × 6.1 km playable terrain (1.5 m height posts) with a 65 km CTX/MOLA backdrop. Built with Unity, C#, and the ECGSYN heartbeat model (telemetry refreshes at 2 Hz, mission stress adds up to +22 bpm and 0.03 mL/kg/min O2 per bpm).
